extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, and researchers interested in internet culture, media ethics, and digital privacy
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the phenomenon of online/public shaming, its types (call-outs, cancellation, doxing, revenge porn, negative reviews, social-status shaming), notable examples, and the ethical, legal, and journalistic debates surrounding it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy concerns / avoid exposing non-public information
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy violation is a major issue in online shaming. Those being shamed may be denied the right to privacy and be subject to defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Websites and users should avoid facilitating the distribution of information that is not part of the public record; exposing private messages, photos, or personally identifiable information raises ethical and legal concerns (David Furlow: sites 'just [give] a forum to people whose statements may not reflect truth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Public shaming imposes punishments that are not proportional to the offenses or alleged offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue shaming often goes beyond the scope of the crime and can destroy lives and careers; evaluators should consider whether the social/media punishment fits the nature and seriousness of the wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative, impartial, and neutral process (fairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public shaming represents the 'justice of the mob' and is not 'deliberative, impartial or neutral' (Martha Nussbaum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective and ethical accountability mechanisms should aim for impartial deliberation and fair procedures rather than mob-driven, emotionally charged condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive shaming with possibility of redemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Public shaming can be constructive, if done right; holding people accountable can correct bad behavior but it has to be paired with a belief in the possibility of redemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents who see value in shaming emphasize designing responses that aim to rehabilitate and allow for moral improvement rather than permanently stigmatizing the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating a 'spoiled identity' (avoid branding as irredeemable)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to avoid what Nussbaum calls a 'spoiled identity': having the public image of someone who is irredeemable and unwelcome in a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaming campaigns and media coverage should avoid permanently branding individuals as beyond redemption; consider long-term social consequences for targets and their communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic responsibility: fact-checking and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists play a key role in expanding the shame and humiliation of targets by relaying claims to a larger audience; often there is very little information about the target, sometimes only a single tweet, yet there is a presumption of guilt and a swift move toward justice, with no process for ascertaining facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should fact-check, evaluate context, avoid amplifying unverified or minimal evidence, and be cautious about reporting that contributes to mob mentality; see referenced 'Journalism and public shaming: Some guidelines' (Poynter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider permanence and scale of social media amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms allow posts to spread quickly and content can be widely circulated and archived through screenshots or reposts, enabling incidents to remain visible long after the original event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors (users, journalists, platforms) should weigh the long-term visibility and archival effects of online shaming before sharing or amplifying accusations; the speed/scale can turn small incidents into major controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish personally identifiable information (doxing prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doxing involves researching and broadcasting personally identifiable information about an individual, often with the intention of harming that person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing home addresses, workplaces, full names, spouse info, credit card details, phone numbers, etc., with intent to harm is ethically wrong and often dangerous; organizations and platforms should prohibit and remove doxing content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent requirement for sexual content; criminality of revenge porn
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-consensual sharing of sexually explicit material in order to humiliate a person (revenge porn) is frequently distributed by ex-partners or hackers; in some jurisdictions, revenge porn is a criminal offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharing explicit images or videos without consent is both an ethical violation and, where the law applies, a criminal act; platforms and users must respect consent and remove such material when reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-review ethics and business response guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: User-generated review sites have been used to publicly shame or punish businesses. Research suggests the quality of the review makes a difference, and some studies show not responding to negative reviews has better outcomes than replying, but businesses should reply to negative reviews to avoid other users blaming the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Businesses should evaluate review quality, craft appropriate responses when beneficial, and consider strategic non-response in some cases; responses should aim to resolve issues without escalating public shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using shaming for revenge, stalking, or blackmail
rubrics_metrics.description: Online shaming may be used to get revenge (e.g., revenge pornography), stalk, blackmail, or to threaten other internet users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using public exposure as a tool for personal revenge or coercion is unethical and may be illegal; evaluators and platforms should distinguish genuine accountability from vindictive or coercive uses of shaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid socioeconomic-status-based shaming (social status shaming harms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social status shaming involves bullying others online due to their socioeconomic status and is utilized as a vessel for social control among classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shaming targeted at individuals because of class or status is an abusive form of social control and should be recognized and discouraged by communities and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require evidence and due process before public condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Often there is a presumption of guilt and swift move toward justice with little information; front-line responses can lack processes for ascertaining facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before amplifying accusations, participants (users, journalists, platforms) should seek corroboration, context, and fair processes to prevent wrongful harm based on incomplete or misleading information (example: Justine Sacco case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of secondary harms (family, dependents, bystanders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public shaming (e.g., Ashley Madison breach) can cause psychological fallout and increase pain for spouses and children; collateral damage extends beyond the individual targeted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider broader social and familial consequences when exposing or amplifying allegations; ethics of disclosure should weigh harms to bystanders and dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms and media should adopt ethical norms for use of hacked/leaked data
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate exists about the ethics of releasing hacked user data (Ashley Madison) and whether naming users is appropriate; security activists and journalists discussed the ethics of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media outlets and platforms should develop norms for handling hacked or leaked documents, including whether to name individuals, how to verify, and how to weigh public interest against privacy and harm.
